title: Evaluating LLM Systems
summary: Measuring whether a generative system is actually good — the hardest and most-asked "AI engineering" skill.

slides.markdown:
Classification has one ground truth per example and a clean accuracy number. Generative text has **many acceptable answers**, so "is this output good" is a genuinely harder measurement problem — and getting it wrong means you ship regressions you never noticed.

- **Reference-based metrics** (BLEU/ROUGE) — cheap but weak for open-ended text.
- **LLM-as-judge** — a model scores another model's output, with its own biases.
- **Golden test sets + online evals** — the two pillars of a real eval strategy.

slides.subTitle: There's no single ground truth
slides.markdown:
A classifier's prediction is either right or wrong against a labeled answer. A generated summary, chat reply, or explanation can be phrased a dozen genuinely correct ways — there's no single string to compare against with exact match. Worse, quality is often multi-dimensional (correct, but also concise, on-tone, and safe) in ways a single scalar score struggles to capture.

This is why evaluating generative systems needs a fundamentally different toolkit than evaluating classifiers — you can't just port over accuracy and F1 and expect them to mean anything.

slides.subTitle: BLEU/ROUGE and why they fall short
slides.markdown:
**BLEU** (translation) and **ROUGE** (summarization) score generated text by measuring n-gram overlap against reference texts — how many word sequences match. Cheap, fast, reproducible, which made them the default for years.

Their core weakness: a correct, fluent answer phrased differently from the reference scores poorly, while a nonsensical answer reusing reference words can score well — they measure surface overlap, not meaning. For open-ended chat or reasoning with no single reference answer, they're often barely informative.

slides.subTitle: Using a model to score another model's output
slides.markdown:
**LLM-as-judge** prompts a (usually stronger) model with the question, the generated answer, and grading criteria, and asks it to score or compare outputs — this scales far better than human review and correlates surprisingly well with human judgment on many tasks, which is why it's become the default for evaluating open-ended generation.

It's not a free lunch: the judge model has its own blind spots and biases, and a judge that's wrong in a consistent, systematic way will silently rubber-stamp a systematic problem in your system rather than catch it.

slides.subTitle: Judge bias toward length and confidence
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "An LLM judge scores answers purely on correctness and quality."

**Why it's wrong:** LLM judges have measurable, documented biases — favoring **longer** answers even when a shorter one is equally correct, and **confident-sounding** phrasing over hedged-but-accurate ones, since those surface features correlate with quality in training data without being quality itself.

**Correct model:** treat judge scores as a signal, not ground truth — calibrate against a human-labeled sample, control for length, and spot-check by hand.

slides.subTitle: Built from real user queries and real failures
slides.markdown:
A **golden test set** is a curated, versioned collection of representative inputs (ideally from real production traffic) paired with what a good answer looks like — used to score every candidate model, prompt, or pipeline change before it ships. Every real production failure found should get added, so a regression that once slipped through can never slip through again.

Without one, "is this prompt change better" is answered by vibes and a few manual spot-checks — which doesn't scale and misses regressions on cases you didn't try.

slides.subTitle: A/B testing and implicit signals
slides.markdown:
Offline evals (golden sets, LLM-as-judge) check quality before shipping; **online evals** measure real users interacting with the live system: explicit thumbs up/down, A/B tests comparing two prompt or model variants on real traffic, and implicit signals like whether the user rephrased their question (a sign the first answer didn't help) or abandoned the session.

Online signals catch things offline evals structurally can't — real query distribution, real edge cases, and whether "better" on your golden set actually translates to a better real-user experience.

slides.subTitle: Offline eval suites vs online production monitoring
slides.markdown:
| | Offline evals | Online evals |
|---|---|---|
| When it runs | Before shipping, on demand | Continuously, on real traffic |
| Catches | Known regressions on curated cases | Unknown issues from real query distribution |
| Speed of signal | Fast — minutes | Slow — needs real usage volume |
| Risk if used alone | Misses cases nobody thought to test | Misses issues before they hit real users |

**How to decide:** use offline evals as the fast pre-ship gate, and online monitoring as the safety net that catches what the gate didn't anticipate — neither one alone is a complete eval strategy.

slides.subTitle: Golden sets need statistical power, not just curation
slides.markdown:
A golden set of 20 hand-picked examples feels thorough but can't reliably detect a change from 85% to 82% pass rate — that 3-point drop is inside the noise of a 20-item sample. As a rule of thumb, distinguishing a few-percentage-point regression with reasonable confidence needs low hundreds of examples, not dozens; detecting a 1-point shift needs thousands.

The practical fix isn't always "collect more examples" — it's matching the test set size to the size of regression you actually need to catch, and being honest that a small set only protects against large, obvious breaks.
